legend: There are n+2%%ZSMJ0%% towns located on a coordinate line, numbered from 0%%ZSMJ1%% to n+1%%ZSMJ2%%. The i%%ZSMJ3%%-th town is located at the point i%%ZSMJ4%%.

You build a radio tower in each of the towns 1,2,…,n%%ZSMJ5%% with probability 12%%ZSMJ6%% (these events are independent). After that, you want to set the signal power on each tower to some integer from 1%%ZSMJ7%% to n%%ZSMJ8%% (signal powers are not necessarily the same, but also not necessarily different). The signal from a tower located in a town i%%ZSMJ9%% with signal power p%%ZSMJ10%% reaches every city c%%ZSMJ11%% such that |c−i|<p%%ZSMJ12%%.
After building the towers, you want to choose signal powers in such a way that:
towns 0%%ZSMJ13%% and n+1%%ZSMJ14%% don't get any signal from the radio towers;
towns 1,2,…,n%%ZSMJ15%% get signal from exactly one radio tower each.

For example, if n=5%%ZSMJ16%%, and you have built the towers in towns 2%%ZSMJ17%%, 4%%ZSMJ18%% and 5%%ZSMJ19%%, you may set the signal power of the tower in town 2%%ZSMJ20%% to 2%%ZSMJ21%%, and the signal power of the towers in towns 4%%ZSMJ22%% and 5%%ZSMJ23%% to 1%%ZSMJ24%%. That way, towns 0%%ZSMJ25%% and n+1%%ZSMJ26%% don't get the signal from any tower, towns 1%%ZSMJ27%%, 2%%ZSMJ28%% and 3%%ZSMJ29%% get the signal from the tower in town 2%%ZSMJ30%%, town 4%%ZSMJ31%% gets the signal from the tower in town 4%%ZSMJ32%%, and town 5%%ZSMJ33%% gets the signal from the tower in town 5%%ZSMJ34%%.
Calculate the probability that, after building the towers, you will have a way to set signal powers to meet all constraints.
input: The first (and only) line of the input contains one integer n%%ZSMJ35%% (1≤n≤2⋅105%%ZSMJ36%%).
output: Print one integer — the probability that there will be a way to set signal powers so that all constraints are met, taken modulo 998244353%%ZSMJ37%%.

Formally, the probability can be expressed as an irreducible fraction xy%%ZSMJ38%%. You have to print the value of x⋅y−1mod%%ZSMJ39%%, where y^{-1}%%ZSMJ40%% is an integer such that y \cdot y^{-1} \bmod 998244353 = 1%%ZSMJ41%%.
note: The real answer for the first example is \frac{1}{4}%%ZSMJ42%%:
with probability \frac{1}{4}%%ZSMJ43%%, the towers are built in both towns 1%%ZSMJ44%% and 2%%ZSMJ45%%, so we can set their signal powers to 1%%ZSMJ46%%.
The real answer for the second example is \frac{1}{4}%%ZSMJ47%%:
with probability \frac{1}{8}%%ZSMJ48%%, the towers are built in towns 1%%ZSMJ49%%, 2%%ZSMJ50%% and 3%%ZSMJ51%%, so we can set their signal powers to 1%%ZSMJ52%%;
with probability \frac{1}{8}%%ZSMJ53%%, only one tower in town 2%%ZSMJ54%% is built, and we can set its signal power to 2%%ZSMJ55%%.

The real answer for the third example is \frac{5}{32}%%ZSMJ56%%. Note that even though the previous explanations used equal signal powers for all towers, it is not necessarily so. For example, if n = 5%%ZSMJ57%% and the towers are built in towns 2%%ZSMJ58%%, 4%%ZSMJ59%% and 5%%ZSMJ60%%, you may set the signal power of the tower in town 2%%ZSMJ61%% to 2%%ZSMJ62%%, and the signal power of the towers in towns 4%%ZSMJ63%% and 5%%ZSMJ64%% to 1%%ZSMJ65%%.
